title: "Module 2 — Organising qualitative data: frequency tables and charts"
subtitle: "Data Description | Part I — Organising data"
date-modified: 2026-10-18
---

**The business question.** The Wandering Fork's owner wants to know:
on which weather conditions does the truck sell most? How concentrated
is the payment-method mix? This module turns a column of categories
into a frequency table and the right chart — the first step in
summarising any qualitative variable. We start with five days small
enough to tally by hand, and only then write the formulas.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this module, you will be able to:

- Build a frequency table with absolute counts ($n_i$), relative
  frequencies ($f_i$), and cumulative frequencies ($N_i^{+}$, $F_i^{+}$)
  for a qualitative variable, by hand.
- Distinguish nominal from ordinal qualitative variables and choose the
  appropriate chart (bar chart for nominal, bar chart with ordered
  categories for ordinal, pie chart only for nominal with few
  categories).
- Read the mode as the modal category.
- Read the frequency and cumulative-frequency formulas aloud as
  sentences, and write them from a description in words.
- Use Excel's `COUNTIF`, `COUNTIFS`, PivotTable counts, and conditional
  formatting to build the table and chart (homework).

## Theory

### Five days, one column of words

Five days of the Harbour truck, as the owner's notebook records them.
The values are a simplified extract chosen so that you can tally
everything by hand.

| Day | `weather` | `satisfaction_rating` (1–5) |
|---|---|---:|
| 1 | Sunny | 4 |
| 2 | Sunny | 5 |
| 3 | Rainy | 3 |
| 4 | Cloudy | 4 |
| 5 | Sunny | 4 |

There is no number to average here: the weather is a word, and even the
rating is a score on a scale. The owner asks you for a one-line summary
of each column. What would you say — and how would you show it on a
single chart?

### Frequency table for a qualitative variable

**Try it.** Tally the `weather` column of the five days above
($n = 5$) and complete the table.

| Category | Tally | Count | Share of days |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| Sunny | ? | ? | ? |
| Cloudy | ? | ? | ? |
| Rainy | ? | ? | ? |
| **Total** | | **?** | **?** |

1. Count the days in each category. Do the counts add up to 5?
2. Divide each count by 5. What do the shares add up to?

Your turn: do the same for the `satisfaction_rating` column.

<details class="answer">
<summary>Check your answer</summary>

| Category | Tally | Count | Share of days |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| Sunny | III | 3 | 3/5 = 60% |
| Cloudy | I | 1 | 1/5 = 20% |
| Rainy | I | 1 | 1/5 = 20% |
| **Total** | | **5** | **100%** |

The counts add up to the number of days, and the shares add up to 100%.

For `satisfaction_rating`: rating 3 → 1 day (20%), rating 4 → 3 days
(60%), rating 5 → 1 day (20%); ratings 1 and 2 → 0 days (0%).

</details>

**Why do the totals come out exactly 5 and 100%?** Every day falls into
exactly one category, so nothing is counted twice and nothing is left
out. That is also why the shares must add up to 1 — the derivation
below makes it precise.

**See it.** The bars below have a height equal to the count of each
category; the share is the count divided by the total, computed by the
page from the same five days.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
forkDays = [
  {weather: "Sunny", rating: 4},
  {weather: "Sunny", rating: 5},
  {weather: "Rainy", rating: 3},
  {weather: "Cloudy", rating: 4},
  {weather: "Sunny", rating: 4}
]
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const cats = ["Sunny", "Cloudy", "Rainy"];
  const counts = cats.map(c => forkDays.filter(d => d.weather === c).length);
  const n = counts.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
  const W = 420, H = 200, base = 150, unit = 30, BLUE = "steelblue";
  let g = "";
  cats.forEach((c, i) => {
    const x = 50 + i * 120, h = counts[i] * unit;
    g += `<rect x="${x}" y="${base - h}" width="80" height="${h}"
      fill="${BLUE}" fill-opacity="0.6" stroke="${BLUE}"/>`;
    g += `<text x="${x + 40}" y="${base - h - 6}" text-anchor="middle"
      fill="currentColor" font-size="13">n = ${counts[i]}
      (${Math.round(100 * counts[i] / n)}%)</text>`;
    g += `<text x="${x + 40}" y="${base + 18}" text-anchor="middle"
      fill="currentColor" font-size="13">${c}</text>`;
  });
  g += `<line x1="40" x2="${W - 10}" y1="${base}" y2="${base}"
    stroke="currentColor"/>`;
  return html`<svg viewBox="0 0 ${W} ${H}" width="100%" role="img"
    aria-label="Bar chart of the weather counts over five days">
    ${g}</svg>`;
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const cats = ["Sunny", "Cloudy", "Rainy"];
  const counts = cats.map(c => forkDays.filter(d => d.weather === c).length);
  const n = counts.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
  return html`<p><em>${cats.map((c, i) => `${c}: ${counts[i]}/${n} =
    ${Math.round(100 * counts[i] / n)}%`).join(" · ")} — total
    ${counts.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0)} days.</em></p>`;
}
```

In plain words: count how many times each category appears, divide by
the total, and you have the share of each category.

::: {.callout-note}
#### Definition — absolute and relative frequency
For a qualitative variable with $k$ categories (modalities) observed on
$n$ individuals, category $i$ has an **absolute frequency** (count)
$n_i$ and a **relative frequency**
$$
f_i = \frac{n_i}{n},
$$
usually reported as a percentage. By construction,
$\sum_{i=1}^{k} n_i = n$ and $\sum_{i=1}^{k} f_i = 1$.
:::

#### Notation decoder: absolute and relative frequency

| Symbol | Read aloud | In our example (`weather`, five days) |
|---|---|---|
| $k$ | "k" | 3 categories (Sunny, Cloudy, Rainy) |
| $n$ | "n" | 5 days |
| $n_i$ | "n sub i" | the count of category $i$, e.g. $n_{\text{Sunny}} = 3$ |
| $f_i$ | "f sub i" | the share of category $i$, e.g. $f_{\text{Sunny}} = 3/5 = 60\%$ |
| $\sum_{i=1}^{k}$ | "add up, for i from 1 to k" | $3+1+1 = 5$, and $0.6+0.2+0.2 = 1$ |

**Whole formula as a sentence:** "the relative frequency of category
$i$ is its count divided by the total number of individuals; the counts
add up to $n$ and the relative frequencies add up to 1."

### Cumulative frequency for ordinal data

**Try it.** The ratings have a natural order (1 < 2 < 3 < 4 < 5).
Complete the running totals for the five days.

| Rating | Count | Running count | Running share |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 0 | ? | ? |
| 2 | 0 | ? | ? |
| 3 | 1 | ? | ? |
| 4 | 3 | ? | ? |
| 5 | 1 | ? | ? |

1. Each running count is the count of that row plus the running count
   of the row above.
2. Divide each running count by 5. What share of days had a rating of 4
   or less?

<details class="answer">
<summary>Check your answer</summary>

| Rating | Count | Running count | Running share |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 0 | 0 | 0% |
| 2 | 0 | 0 | 0% |
| 3 | 1 | 1 | 20% |
| 4 | 3 | 4 | 80% |
| 5 | 1 | 5 | 100% |

80% of the days had a rating of 4 or less. The last running count is
always $n = 5$ and the last running share is always 100%.

</details>

**See it.** Each bar of the figure below is a rating level, in order;
the number under each bar is the running total of the bar heights from
the left, computed from the same five days.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const levels = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5];
  const counts = levels.map(l => forkDays.filter(d => d.rating === l).length);
  const n = counts.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
  let run = 0;
  const cum = counts.map(c => (run += c));
  const W = 420, H = 230, base = 150, unit = 30, BLUE = "steelblue";
  let g = "";
  levels.forEach((l, i) => {
    const x = 40 + i * 72, h = counts[i] * unit;
    g += `<rect x="${x}" y="${base - h}" width="50" height="${h}"
      fill="${BLUE}" fill-opacity="0.6" stroke="${BLUE}"/>`;
    g += `<text x="${x + 25}" y="${base - h - 6}" text-anchor="middle"
      fill="currentColor" font-size="13">${counts[i]}</text>`;
    g += `<text x="${x + 25}" y="${base + 18}" text-anchor="middle"
      fill="currentColor" font-size="13">rating ${l}</text>`;
    g += `<text x="${x + 25}" y="${base + 40}" text-anchor="middle"
      fill="darkorange" font-size="13">N = ${cum[i]}
      (${Math.round(100 * cum[i] / n)}%)</text>`;
  });
  g += `<line x1="30" x2="${W - 10}" y1="${base}" y2="${base}"
    stroke="currentColor"/>`;
  return html`<svg viewBox="0 0 ${W} ${H}" width="100%" role="img"
    aria-label="Bar chart of ratings in order with running totals">
    ${g}</svg>`;
}
```

In plain words: for ordinal data like `satisfaction_rating` (1 < 2 < 3
< 4 < 5), you can ask "what share of days had a rating of 3 or less?"
and the cumulative frequency answers it.

::: {.callout-tip}
#### Formula — cumulative frequency (ordinal only)
If the categories have a natural order (ordinal), you can cumulate:
$$
N_i^{+} = \sum_{j=1}^{i} n_j,
\qquad
F_i^{+} = \frac{N_i^{+}}{n}.
$$
$N_i^{+}$ is the running total of counts up to and including category
$i$; $F_i^{+}$ is the running share. For nominal data, cumulative
frequencies are meaningless because there is no order.
:::

#### Notation decoder: cumulative frequency

| Symbol | Read aloud | In our example (ratings, five days) |
|---|---|---|
| $n_j$ | "n sub j" | the count of rating $j$, e.g. $n_4 = 3$ |
| $\sum_{j=1}^{i}$ | "add up, for j from 1 to i" | stop at the rating $i$ you ask about |
| $N_i^{+}$ | "capital N sub i plus" | the running count: $N_4^{+} = 0+0+1+3 = 4$ |
| $n$ | "n" | 5 days |
| $F_i^{+}$ | "capital F sub i plus" | the running share: $F_4^{+} = 4/5 = 80\%$ |

**Whole formula as a sentence:** "the cumulative count up to category
$i$ is the sum of the counts of categories 1 through $i$; the
cumulative frequency is that running count divided by the total."

### Nominal vs ordinal — choosing the chart

**Try it.** Decide, for each column, whether it is nominal or ordinal,
and which chart you would use.

| Column | Nominal or ordinal? | Chart? |
|---|---|---|
| `weather` (Sunny, Cloudy, Rainy) | ? | ? |
| `satisfaction_rating` (1 to 5) | ? | ? |

Then compute the angle of the Sunny slice if you drew a pie chart of
the five days.

<details class="answer">
<summary>Check your answer</summary>

| Column | Nominal or ordinal? | Chart? |
|---|---|---|
| `weather` | nominal (no order) | bar chart, or pie chart (3 categories) |
| `satisfaction_rating` | ordinal (1 < … < 5) | bar chart, categories in order 1 to 5 |

Sunny's share is 60%, so its slice spans $0.6 \times 360° = 216°$
(Cloudy and Rainy: $72°$ each; $216°+72°+72° = 360°$).

</details>

**See it.** The two bar charts above are the right pictures: the
weather bars can be in any order, while the rating bars must follow
1 to 5, because the running totals only make sense in that order. A
pie chart has no starting point, so it could not show that order.

In plain words: a pie chart slices a circle; it has no beginning or
end, so it cannot show order. A bar chart can be sorted by the
meaningful order of the categories.

::: {.callout-note}
#### Definition — nominal vs ordinal charts
- **Nominal** (no order): bar chart (categories in any order) or pie
  chart (if few categories). The bar order is arbitrary; alphabetical
  or by frequency are common choices.
- **Ordinal** (natural order): bar chart with categories **in their
  natural order**. A pie chart is not appropriate because it ignores
  the order.
:::

### The mode

**Try it.** In the two frequency tables you built, which category has
the highest count? Is it the same kind of answer for `weather` and for
`satisfaction_rating`?

<details class="answer">
<summary>Check your answer</summary>

`weather`: Sunny (3 days). `satisfaction_rating`: 4 (3 days). In both
cases the answer is a **category**, not a number computed from the
data: you cannot average words, but you can always name the most
common one.

</details>

**See it.** In both bar charts above, the mode is the tallest bar.

In plain words: the mode is the "most common" category.

::: {.callout-tip}
#### Definition — mode of a qualitative variable
The **mode** is the category with the highest absolute frequency $n_i$.
For a frequency table, it is simply the row with the largest count.
:::

#### Notation decoder: mode of a qualitative variable

| Symbol | Read aloud | In our example (five days) |
|---|---|---|
| $n_i$ | "n sub i" | the count of category $i$: 3, 1, 1 for Sunny, Cloudy, Rainy |
| mode | "the modal category" | Sunny, the row with the largest $n_i$ |

**Whole formula as a sentence:** "the mode is the category whose
absolute frequency is the largest."

## Worked example

We use the **Harbour 30-day subset** (sheet `harbour_30d`). The
variable `weather` (nominal, 3 categories) and `satisfaction_rating`
(ordinal, 5 categories) are summarised below.

### `weather` (nominal, $n=30$)

| Category | $n_i$ | $f_i$ (%) |
|---|---:|---:|
| Sunny | 13 | 43.3 |
| Cloudy | 12 | 40.0 |
| Rainy | 5 | 16.7 |
| **Total** | **30** | **100.0** |

**Step 1 — counts.** Each day's `weather` value is tallied: 13 Sunny,
12 Cloudy, 5 Rainy; $13+12+5=30=n$. ✓

**Step 2 — relative frequencies.** $f_{\text{Sunny}} = 13/30 = 43.3\%$,
$f_{\text{Cloudy}} = 12/30 = 40.0\%$, $f_{\text{Rainy}} = 5/30 = 16.7\%$;
the three sum to $100.0\%$.

**Step 3 — choosing a chart.** `weather` is nominal with only 3
categories: both a **bar chart** (one bar per category, height = count
or frequency) and a **pie chart** (one slice per category, angle $=
f_i \times 360°$) are appropriate. Sunny's slice spans
$0.433 \times 360° \approx 156°$; Cloudy's $\approx 144°$; Rainy's
$\approx 60°$.

**Step 4 — mode.** The modal category is **Sunny** ($n_i = 13$).

### `satisfaction_rating` (ordinal, $n=30$)

| Rating | $n_i$ | $f_i$ (%) | $N_i^{+}$ | $F_i^{+}$ (%) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 0 | 0.0 | 0 | 0.0 |
| 2 | 6 | 20.0 | 6 | 20.0 |
| 3 | 6 | 20.0 | 12 | 40.0 |
| 4 | 16 | 53.3 | 28 | 93.3 |
| 5 | 2 | 6.7 | 30 | 100.0 |

**Step 1 — counts and shares.** Tallied from the 30 days. No day was
rated 1, but the category stays in the table with a count of 0: an
ordinal scale keeps all its levels.

**Step 2 — cumulative frequencies.** $N_i^{+}$ and $F_i^{+}$ are the
running totals. For example, $F_3^{+} = 40.0\%$ means 40% of days had a
rating of 3 or less.

**Step 3 — chart.** A **bar chart** with categories in order 1, 2, 3,
4, 5. The bars show the distribution's shape: more than half of the
days are rated 4.

**Step 4 — mode.** The modal category is **4** ($n_i = 16$).

## Proof / derivation

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
#### Derivation — relative frequencies always sum to 1 (click to expand)
Let a qualitative variable have $k$ categories with counts
$n_1, \dots, n_k$, and let $n = \sum_{i=1}^{k} n_i$ be the total
number of individuals (every individual falls into exactly one
category, so the counts partition the population — the same
partition idea used for PivotTable groups in Module 1). Then
$$
\sum_{i=1}^{k} f_i = \sum_{i=1}^{k} \frac{n_i}{n}
= \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{k} n_i = \frac{n}{n} = 1.
$$
For "The Wandering Fork" `weather`:
$f_{\text{Sunny}}+f_{\text{Cloudy}}+f_{\text{Rainy}}
= 0.433+0.400+0.167 = 1.000$. ✓
:::

## Visual intuition

The pie chart's geometry makes the frequency-sum-to-1 property
*visible*: the three slices' angles, $156°+144°+60°=360°$, always
complete a full circle no matter how the 30 days split across
Sunny/Cloudy/Rainy — exactly as the algebra above guarantees.

For ordinal data, the bar chart with ordered categories makes the
cumulative frequency visible: the running total of bar heights up to
category $i$ is exactly $N_i^{+}$.

## Exercises

All exercises below are done by hand; the Excel ones are in the
[homework](#homework-excel-lab).

::: {#exr-rating-table name="Frequency table for `satisfaction_rating`"}
Using the worked-example table for `satisfaction_rating`, verify that
the cumulative frequencies $N_i^{+}$ and $F_i^{+}$ are correct. What
percentage of days had a rating of 3 or less?

<details class="answer">
<summary>Solution</summary>

$F_3^{+} = 40.0\%$ (from the table). Check:
$N_3^{+} = 0+6+6 = 12$; $12/30 = 0.400 = 40.0\%$.

</details>
:::

::: {#exr-choosing-chart name="Choosing the right chart"}
Which chart type(s) would you use for `weather`, and why would a
**line chart** be a poor choice?

<details class="answer">
<summary>Solution</summary>

A bar chart or a pie chart, because `weather` is
nominal qualitative with no meaningful order between Sunny, Cloudy,
and Rainy. A line chart implies a continuous progression *between*
consecutive categories, which does not exist here — connecting
"Sunny" to "Cloudy" to "Rainy" with a line would suggest an ordering
that isn't real.

</details>
:::

::: {#exr-pie-slice-angle name="Pie-slice angle"}
What angle does Cloudy's pie slice occupy, and what percentage of the
circle's area does it represent?

<details class="answer">
<summary>Solution</summary>

Angle $= f_{\text{Cloudy}} \times 360° = 0.400 \times
360° = 144°$. Since a pie chart's slice area is proportional to its
angle, Cloudy also represents $40.0\%$ of the circle's area — matching
its relative frequency exactly, by construction.

</details>
:::

::: {#exr-formula-words name="Formula to words"}
Read $F_i^{+} = \dfrac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{i} n_j$ aloud as one sentence.
Which indicator is it, and for which kind of variable does it make
sense?

<details class="answer">
<summary>Solution</summary>

"The cumulative relative frequency up to category $i$ is the sum of
the counts of categories 1 through $i$, divided by the total number
$n$ of individuals." It is the running share, and it only makes sense
for **ordinal** variables, where the categories have an order.

</details>
:::

::: {#exr-words-formula name="Words to formula"}
Write in symbols: (a) "the share of category $i$ is its count divided
by the total"; (b) "the counts of the $k$ categories add up to the
total"; (c) "the running count up to category $i$".

<details class="answer">
<summary>Solution</summary>

(a) $f_i = \dfrac{n_i}{n}$. (b) $\sum_{i=1}^{k} n_i = n$.
(c) $N_i^{+} = \sum_{j=1}^{i} n_j$.

</details>
:::

## Common mistakes

::: {.callout-warning}
#### Watch out
- **Using a pie chart for ordinal data.** A pie chart destroys the
  order information; use a bar chart with categories in their natural
  order.
- **Cumulative frequencies for nominal data.** $N_i^{+}$ and $F_i^{+}$
  only make sense when the categories have a natural order.
- **Forgetting that percentages may not sum to exactly 100% due to
  rounding.** $43.3\% + 40.0\% + 16.7\% = 100.0\%$ here, but with more
  categories you might get $99.9\%$ or $100.1\%$ — this is a rounding
  artifact, not an error.
- **Using `COUNT` instead of `COUNTA` for text categories.** `COUNT`
  only counts numbers; `COUNTA` counts everything non-empty.
:::

## Exit check

Five minutes, no calculator needed.

1. In one sentence, what does a relative frequency $f_i$ measure?
2. Why are cumulative frequencies meaningless for `weather`?
3. Read $f_i = n_i / n$ aloud as a sentence.
4. Five days are rated 1, 2, 2, 4, 5. Build the table of counts and
   running shares, and give the mode.
5. Which chart would you use for the five ratings, and why not a pie
   chart?

<details class="answer">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. The share of the $n$ individuals that fall into category $i$: its
   count divided by the total.
2. `weather` is nominal: there is no order, so "running total up to
   Rainy" depends on an arbitrary listing order.
3. "The relative frequency of category $i$ is its count divided by the
   total number of individuals."
4. Counts for ratings 1 to 5: 1, 2, 0, 1, 1. Running counts: 1, 3, 3,
   4, 5; running shares: 20%, 60%, 60%, 80%, 100%. The mode is rating
   2 (2 days).
5. A bar chart with the ratings in the order 1 to 5: the rating is
   ordinal, and a pie chart has no starting point, so it cannot show
   the order.

</details>

## Homework — Excel lab

Reproduce, in Excel, every table you built by hand in class, with
`COUNTIF`, `COUNTIFS`, running sums, a PivotTable and conditional
formatting, then apply them to the full dataset.

**Estimated time:** about 50–60 minutes. Any spreadsheet application
works, at home or in a campus computer room.

**Follow-up:** a 10-minute debrief at the start of
[Module 3](module-03.qmd). Bring your Step 0 results and any question
on Homework 1–3.

### Using Excel

The sheet `harbour_30d` of `wandering-fork.xlsx` has the data. The
complete list of function names, with their French equivalents, is on
the [Excel functions](excel-functions.qmd) page.

| Concept | Excel function / steps |
|---|---|
| Count one category | `=COUNTIF(range, "Sunny")` |
| Count with several criteria | `=COUNTIFS(range1, criterion1, range2, criterion2, …)` |
| Relative frequency | `=count/COUNT(range)` (or `/COUNTA` for text data) |
| Cumulative count | First row `=count`; below `=above + current` (running sum) |
| Cumulative share | `=cumulative_count/COUNT(range)` |
| Bar chart | Select the summary table → **Insert → Chart → Clustered Column** |
| Pie chart (nominal only) | Select the summary table → **Insert → Chart → Pie** |
| PivotTable counts | **Insert → PivotTable**, put the qualitative field in **Rows** and the same field (or any non-empty field) in **Values** set to *Count* |
| Conditional formatting | Select the count column → **Home → Conditional Formatting → Highlight Cell Rules → Greater Than** (or a custom formula) |

For the **full table** (120 days per franchise) use the Excel Table
`tblFork` and add the franchise as one more condition, for example
`=COUNTIFS(tblFork[franchise],"Harbour",tblFork[weather],"Sunny")`.

### Step 0 — check your class results

1. Type the five weather values (Sunny, Sunny, Rainy, Cloudy, Sunny) in
   `A2:A6` and the five ratings (4, 5, 3, 4, 4) in `B2:B6`.
2. Count each weather category with `=COUNTIF($A$2:$A$6, "Sunny")`
   (and the same for Cloudy and Rainy), then divide by
   `=COUNTA($A$2:$A$6)`.
3. Count each rating level 1 to 5 with `=COUNTIF($B$2:$B$6, 1)` (and so
   on), then build the running count (`=above + current`) and the
   running share.
4. Compare every result with your hand computation.

<details class="answer">
<summary>Expected results</summary>

| Category | Count | Share |
|---|---:|---:|
| Sunny | 3 | 60% |
| Cloudy | 1 | 20% |
| Rainy | 1 | 20% |

| Rating | Count | Running count | Running share |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 0 | 0 | 0% |
| 2 | 0 | 0 | 0% |
| 3 | 1 | 1 | 20% |
| 4 | 3 | 4 | 80% |
| 5 | 1 | 5 | 100% |

</details>

### Homework 1 (Excel) — Build the frequency table with `COUNTIFS`

In `wandering-fork.xlsx`, filter `franchise` to "Harbour" and use
`COUNTIFS` to build the frequency table for `weather` over all 120
days. What are the counts and relative frequencies?

<details class="answer">
<summary>Solution</summary>

Formula for Sunny:
`=COUNTIFS(tblFork[franchise],"Harbour",tblFork[weather],"Sunny")`.
You should obtain: Sunny 53 (44.2%), Cloudy 42 (35.0%), Rainy 25
(20.8%). The proportions are close to the 30-day subset (43.3%, 40.0%,
16.7%) because the data were generated with the same weather
probabilities; the gaps of a few points are ordinary chance variation.

</details>

### Homework 2 (Excel) — PivotTable and conditional formatting

Build a PivotTable for `satisfaction_rating` (Harbour, 120 days) with
the rating in **Rows** and **Count of rating** in **Values**. Apply
conditional formatting to highlight the modal category (the one with
the highest count). What is the mode?

<details class="answer">
<summary>Solution</summary>

The PivotTable gives counts: 1→4, 2→21, 3→40, 4→45,
5→10 (total 120). The mode is **4** (45 days). Conditional formatting
rule: `=B2=MAX($B$2:$B$6)` applied to the count column highlights the
row for rating 4.

</details>

### Homework 3 (Excel) — Campus weather comparison

Build the `weather` frequency table for **Campus** (120 days) using
`COUNTIFS` on `tblFork`. Compare the relative frequencies with
Harbour's. Are they similar?

<details class="answer">
<summary>Solution</summary>

Campus: Sunny 50 (41.7%), Cloudy 48 (40.0%), Rainy 22
(18.3%). The proportions are similar to Harbour's (44.2%, 35.0%,
20.8%) because both franchises were generated with the same weather
probabilities; the remaining differences are chance variation.

</details>
